heard: You're a fraud investigator, and someone at this company is faking expenses. Here's how you catch them. Ignore the amounts. Write down only the first digit of each one, $1 ,280. That's a one. Count them. In honest books, about 30 % start with a one. Only about 5 % start with a nine. Money grows by percent. To get from 100 to 200, it has to double. From 900 to 1 ,000, it only needs 11 % more. So amounts sit on one far longer. It works when amounts run from tens to thousands, like expenses do. Now your company's approval limit is $5 ,000. Anything above it needs a manager. Check one clerk. Almost a third of their expenses start with a four. Honest books, under 10%. Zoom in, 4 ,850. 4 ,920, 4 ,975. Everyone sits just under the limit. Uh -oh, you have 10 ,000 expenses and no time. You don't need it. The digits point to one clerk and 50 claims. And there you have it. One digit caught them and you never opened the other 9 ,950 receipts. This is Benford's Law. Simon Newcomb noticed it in 1881. And auditors still use it today. In honest books, what share of amounts start with a two? Tell me below.
